Article Title: Parliament panel to meet social media platforms over online safety, privacy
Article Text:
Parliament panel summons social media platforms at 4 pm

NEW DELHI: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology will meet representatives of major social media platforms, including Meta, X, Snapchat and Google on Monday to discuss online safety, user privacy and compliance with government rules.The meeting, scheduled for 4 pm, will focus on the digital safety of women and children, protection of data belonging to farmers, rural residents, labourers and the general public and how social media companies comply with laws related to public order.BJP MP and committee chairperson Nishikant Dubey said the platforms had been summoned to explain the steps they were taking to safeguard user privacy and ensure compliance with government regulations."On 3 August 2026 at 4 PM, our Parliamentary Committee on IT and Communication has summoned Meta (Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp), X (Twitter), Snapchat, and Google," Dubey said."How will the privacy of women, children, farmers, rural folks, labourers, and the general public be protected? How do these companies ensure the government's public order?" he added.The meeting comes days after Meta briefly removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Facebook video on action against examination paper leaks before restoring it.Meta later said the video had been removed due to a technical error."The content was removed in error and has since been restored," a Meta spokesperson said.The video, released on July 23, was PM Modi's first direct address to Gen Z during the 36-day-long Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led agitation over alleged irregularities in the NEET-UG 2026 examination.In the address, PM Modi assured students that the government would strengthen the legal framework against paper leaks by introducing stricter punishment and Special Fast-Track Courts.The Centre later introduced the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, proposing imprisonment of up to 10 years, higher monetary penalties and Special Fast-Track Courts for offences under the law.The student agitation ended on July 25 after Dharmendra Pradhan resigned as education minister. The Centre also reached an understanding with the CJP and activist Sonam Wangchuk to withdraw cases against protesters, prevent police intimidation and bring in stronger anti-paper leak legislation.
Article Summary: Parliament panel summons social media platforms at 4 pm on Monday. Meeting will focus on digital safety of women and children, protection of data belonging to farmers, rural residents, labourers and the general public. Meta briefly removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Facebook video on action against examination paper leaks before restoring it.

Article Title: Live-in partners can seek protection under Section 498A, says Supreme Court
Article Text:
Section 498A prescribes imprisonment of up to three years and a fine for subjecting a woman to cruelty

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court said Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, which deals with cruelty by a husband or his relatives, would also apply to partners in live-in relationships, expanding the scope of the provision beyond formally married couples. The court said the law must evolve with changing social realities and ensure protection for individuals facing harassment in live-in relationships.The bench observed that legal safeguards against cruelty should not be restricted to marriage alone. It also clarified that live-in partners need not necessarily be a man and a woman, recognising that such relationships may take different forms.Section 498A prescribes imprisonment of up to three years and a fine for subjecting a woman to cruelty. The law defines cruelty as conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide, cause serious physical or mental harm, or harassment aimed at coercing unlawful demands for property or valuable security, including dowry.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court said Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code would also apply to partners in live-in relationships. The court said the law must evolve with changing social realities. The bench observed that legal safeguards against cruelty should not be restricted to marriage alone.

Article Title: Kunal Kamra shifts three Whitefield shows following opposition by 'Hindutva activists'
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Stand-up comedian Kunal Kamra has cancelled his scheduled shows in Bengaluru's Whitefield after protests by Hindutva activists, police said on Monday.Kamra visited the Whitefield police station on Sunday and informed the authorities that he would not go ahead with the performances at the venue."He (Kamra) came to the police station and informed that he has decided to cancel the event scheduled in Whitefield due to the opposition by Hindutva activists," a senior police officer said.The development comes days after the Hindu Rashtra Samanvaya Samiti submitted a petition to the Bengaluru Police seeking cancellation of Kamra's August 3 stand-up show at URU Whitefield.The group alleged that the comedian had disrespected Hindu deities and claimed the event could pose a threat to law and order and religious harmony.Kamra later announced on X that his shows scheduled for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday had been shifted to a venue in Koramangala.He also said that BookMyShow would process refunds for tickets booked for the Whitefield shows and requested audiences to book tickets for the Koramangala venue, while noting that seating there is limited.Kamra has frequently courted controversy over his stand-up routines and public remarks.Last year, Shiv Sena workers vandalised the studio and hotel premises where he had performed after taking objection to his remarks.In 2020, Kamra sparked another controversy after confronting a journalist on an IndiGo flight from Mumbai to Lucknow. He shared a video of the incident on X, after which IndiGo, SpiceJet, GoAir and Air India barred him from flying with their airlines.
Article Summary: Kunal Kamra has cancelled his scheduled shows in Bengaluru's Whitefield after protests by Hindutva activists. Hindu Rashtra Samanvaya Samiti submitted a petition to the Bengaluru Police seeking cancellation of Kamra's August 3 show at URU Whitefield.

Article Title: 2 strategic satellites sit at spaceport as govt nod eludes Isro
Article Text:
GSLV-Mk2

BENGALURU: Two strategically important satellites, NVS-03 and Gisat-1A, have been sitting at India’s spaceport in Sriharikota for weeks, awaiting govt approval for launch. Also waiting is a GSLV-Mk2 rocket, whose propellant filling was halted midway after launch clearance failed to come through, multiple sources told TOI.The delay comes even as the govt is yet to publicly disclose detailed findings into the failures of two PSLV missions — May 18, 2025 and Jan 12, 2026 — that have effectively slowed India’s launch programme across vehicle families.Sources said NVS-03, the next satellite in India's second-generation NavIC navigation constellation, and GISAT-1A or EOS-05, an advanced geo-imaging satellite capable of near real-time observation of the Indian landmass, have both completed most pre-launch preparations and are ready for flight.The GSLV-Mk2 at the spaceport was designated for one of the missions (NVS-03 or Gisat-1A). The pause in launch follows a difficult year for Isro. On Jan 12, PSLV-C62 failed to place its payloads into orbit after a disruption in the third stage (PS3).Eight months before that, PSLV-C61 had also failed because of what Isro has described only as a “pressure drop in PS3”. Apart from these brief descriptions, neither the department of space (DoS) nor the Govt has released detailed failure reports.Union minister Jitendra Singh recently said in Bengaluru that the failure analysis committee investigating the PSLV-C62 mission had identified the cause of the anomaly but that the findings “could not be disclosed publicly”.The apparent caution extending beyond PSLV has befuddled even those within the Department of Space, which is already battling low morale. Officials familiar with the matter said no launches have been cleared while the govt reviews the situation.Pointing out that the issues identified so far relate specifically to the PSLV’s third stage and do not directly involve either the GSLV or the LVM-3, one insider said: “We don’t get the logic. It’s like telling us not to take our cars out because our bike had an issue in its previous outing.” The person argued that GSLV and LVM rockets don’t borrow anything from the PSLV third stage.The delay is particularly significant because both satellites have strategic roles. NVS-03 is expected to be one step in reviving the now-defunct NavIC navigation constellation. Even the govt last week admitted that with just three functional satellites, the NavIC programme has failed to deliver navigation services for lack of satellites.Gisat-1A, meanwhile, revives a mission that has suffered repeated setbacks. The original Gisat-1, India’s first geostationary Earth observation satellite designed to provide frequent imaging of the subcontinent, was first delayed in 2020 before being lost during the GSLV-F10 mission in Aug 2021 after the cryogenic upper stage failed to ignite. The replacement spacecraft is expected to provide near real-time imaging for disaster management, agriculture, forestry, environmental monitoring and national security.The govt’s caution follows another major setback that was investigated in detail. Isro, in Feb this year, released partial findings into the Jan 2025 NVS-02 anomaly, concluding that the spacecraft failed to reach its intended orbit because the drive signal never reached the pyro valve in the oxidiser line during orbit-raising manoeuvres.The agency said corrective measures had since been implemented and successfully validated on the CMS-03 mission launched aboard LVM-3 in Nov 2025. For now, however, even as hardware, satellites and launch vehicles stand ready at the spaceport, India’s next launches remain on hold, with no indication of when the govt will authorise launches to resume.
Article Summary: Two strategically important satellites, NVS-03 and Gisat-1A, have been sitting at India’s spaceport in Sriharikota for weeks, awaiting govt approval for launch. Also waiting is a GSLV-Mk2 rocket, whose propellant filling was halted midway after launch clearance failed to come through.

Article Title: SC warns Punjab for ignoring 15-yr-old ruling on dues to Himachal Pradesh
Article Text:
Inter-state row

NEW DELHI: Punjab govt's stiff resistance to attorney general R Venkataramani's proposal for amicable implementation of a 15-year-old Supreme Court decree settling Bhakra Nangal and Beas power dues since 1966 in favour of Himachal Pradesh made SC observe, "The state has a habit of defying decrees and old habits die hard. "Venkataramani told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that he had extensive consultations with Punjab, Haryana, Himachal and Union ministry of power after getting the records examined by CAG for independent determination of the historical capital cost liability."...a mutually workable settlement framework has been evolved. It envisages a cashless settlement, wherein the respective claims and liabilities are proposed to be adjusted through in-kind settlement of energy arrears and set-off of capital cost liability, thereby obviating the need for any direct financial transaction between the states," the AG said.Senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Balbir Singh, appearing for Himachal and Haryana, respectively, said they were agreeable with the AG's settlement proposal for implementation of the decree, which was passed by the SC in 2011 on an original suit filed by Himachal 30 years ago seeking settlement of assets on division of Punjab in 1966.For Punjab, senior advocate Nidhesh Gupta said the state had key concerns over workability of the AG's proposal and said the state would stand to lose substantially.Given the fact that it is a 15-year-old decree passed on a 30-year-old original suit seeking resolution of a 60-year-old inter-state dispute, the bench said, "Your state has a habit of defying decrees...""There is a decree in Himachal's favour. When we order implement, it will be with interest from 2011. We will not allow them to be deprived of the fruits of the decree. If you settle, it is well and good. Otherwise, be ready for consequences." It posted the matter for hearing on Aug 12.In its July 30 order, the bench said, "While the states of Himachal and Haryana have graciously agreed in principle to the proposal, the state of Punjab has raised objections thereto. In the interest of justice, two weeks time is granted to Punjab to reconsider and clarify its stand."The AG's proposal had said, "Punjab and Haryana will provide 13,066 MU of energy arrears to HP at 871 MU per annum over 15 lean seasons (Oct-March), in the inter-se ratio of 58:42 (Bhakra Nangal project) and 60:40 (Beas projects). HP to pay BBMB-determined charges for the year in which each tranche is received."HP's liability (7.19% of composite Punjab) towards the capital cost of Bhakra Nangal and Beas projects - being the unreimbursed share of loan servicing by Punjab and Haryana since 1966-67 - be assessed at Rs 420.7 crore (Punjab: Rs 249.2 crore; Haryana: Rs 171.5 crore). The capital cost liability could be considered to set off against part of HP's energy arrear receivables.At the rate of Rs 3.85 per unit, the units to be offset is approximately 1093 MUs. "SC on Sept 27, 2011 (Justices R V Raveendran and A K Patnaik) had decreed the suit in favour of HP by ruling, "The state is entitled to 7.19% of the power of the composite state of Punjab from the Bhakra Nangal project with effect from Nov 1, 1966, and from Beas project with effect from the dates of production in Unit I and Unit II."
Article Summary: Punjab govt's stiff resistance to amicable implementation of 15-year-old Supreme Court decree. Decree settled Bhakra Nangal and Beas power dues since 1966 in favour of Himachal Pradesh. "The state has a habit of defying decrees and old habits die hard," says SC.

Article Title: NTA floats tender to secure offices, exam material 24x7
Article Text:
The agency has floated a tender estimated at Rs 7.5 crore to hire a security firm for its headquarters at Minto Road, regional office in Okhla and other notified locations.

Bidders for NTA tender will have to deposit 15 lakh as earnest money

NEW DELHI: After a paper leak exposed weak links in India’s biggest entrance examination, National Testing Agency NTA ) is moving to put its premises, confidential records and examination material under round-the-clock watch. The agency has floated a tender estimated at Rs 7.5 crore to hire a security firm for its headquarters at Minto Road, regional office in Okhla and other notified locations.Issued on July 25, the tender is part of a procurement exercise covering security, housekeeping and examination-grade printing. Together, the bids signal an attempt to tighten controls across the examination chain — from printing and storage to access control and protection of digital infrastructure. The security contract will initially run for two years and may be extended twice by a year each. Bids can be submitted until 3 pm on Aug 17. The printing-services tender closes on Aug 20.The selected agency will watch over NTA employees, visitors, premises, confidential examination material, server rooms, strong rooms, warehouses, record rooms and other sensitive facilities. It will regulate entry and exit, verify staff and visitors, maintain logs and ensure that “only authorised persons enter restricted areas”.The security apparatus will include door-frame and hand-held metal detectors, GPS-enabled guard patrol tracking, biometric attendance and digital incident-reporting systems.NTA has moved away from choosing a bidder mainly on cost basis. Citing the “sensitive nature of NTA’s examination ecosystem and confidentiality requirements”, it has adopted the quality-and-cost based selection model. Technical capability will carry 70% weightage and the financial bid 30%. Only agencies securing at least 70 marks in the technical assessment will reach the financial round.Bidders must have at least five years’ experience in professional security, an average annual turnover of Rs 10 crore in past three financial years and must have done prior work at high-security establishments such as central govt institutions, examination agencies, universities, airports, hospitals or metro systems.The contract value excludes GST. Bidders must deposit Rs 15 lakh as earnest money, while the successful agency will furnish performance security equal to 5% of the contract value.Confidentiality is mandatory. The service provider and its personnel must protect information relating to examination material, security arrangements and IT systems even after the contract ends.The tender has been floated amid efforts to rebuild public confidence after the NEET controversy and have a foolproof system in place against paper leaks. The exercise suggests that NTA is treating security as a process in which every access point can become a vulnerability.
Article Summary: National Testing Agency NTA is moving to put its premises, confidential records and examination material under round-the-clock watch. The agency has floated a tender estimated at Rs 7.5 crore to hire a security firm for its headquarters at Minto Road, regional office in Okhla and other notified locations. Bids can be submitted until 3 pm on Aug 17.

Article Title: 10,000 cases pending in SC for 10 yrs, 80,000 in HCs for 30 yrs
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Improving court infrastructure and integration of technology in the justice delivery system with an outlay of more than Rs 9,800 crore since 2011 have had little impact on disposal of cases pending for several decades. More than 10,000 cases are pending in the Supreme Court for over 10 years — including 558 pending for over 20 years, and 26 cases for 30 years. In the 25 high courts across the country, over 80,000 cases are pending for over three decades.In a written response to a question in Parliament last week, law minister Arjun Ram Meghwal put the onus of disposal of cases on the judiciary, which has not fixed a time frame for their disposal.He further said: “Timely disposal of cases in courts depends on several factors which, inter-alia, include availability of adequate number of judges and judicial officers, supporting court staff and physical infrastructure, complexity of facts involved, nature of evidence, cooperation of stakeholders viz bar, investigation agencies, witnesses, litigants and proper application of rules and procedures.While the apex court has been prompt in appointing judges against vacancies, the situation in 25 high courts and subordinate courts is not the same.The HCs currently have 341 vacancies of judges against a sanctioned strength of 1,122. The subordinate courts have 7,311 vacancies against an approved strength of 30,868 judges.The law minister blamed the respective HC collegiums for not following the timeline prescribed for initiating recommendation for appointments of judges for the HCs, the primary reason behind large vacancies. The HC collegium comprises the chief justice and two senior-most judges of the high court. For the SC, the recommendation for the appointment of judges is initiated by the Chief Justice of India.“Arrears Committees have been set up in all 25 high courts and the district courts to clear cases pending for more than five years. The govt has also enacted the New Criminal Laws 2023, Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2018, Commercial Courts (Amendment) Act, 2018, Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 with a view to reduce pendency,” Meghwal said.
Article Summary: More than 10,000 cases are pending in the Supreme Court for over 10 years. In the 25 high courts across the country, over 80,000 Cases are pending for over three decades. Law minister Arjun Ram Meghwal put the onus of disposal of cases on the judiciary.

Article Title: Educated but unemployed: Inside India's broken jobs market and why the 'cockroaches' are fed up
Article Text:
India's un-employment crisis and helplessness of modern life. (Representative image)

And at its heart lies a simple question. What happens when an economy produces millions of graduates every year but fails to create enough quality jobs?

India's employment challenge



The problem isn't just unemployment, it's job quality



Why educated youth feel left behind

India's employment paradox



Is India creating enough jobs?



The informal sector is slowing too



India's employment quality lags behind peers



The real issue is the lack of decent employment opportunities. We saw this clearly in Uttar Pradesh in 2017, when more than two lakh people applied for peon posts. Many applicants held qualifications such as PhDs, MTech, BTech, MCom and BCom degrees. When highly educated people apply for peon jobs, it shows they are unable to find work that matches their qualifications. Arun Kumar

AI adds a new challenge



India's demographic dividend at a crossroads



When NEET became the tipping point

Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis transformed an ordinary man into a giant insect to explore alienation, helplessness and the dehumanising pressures of modern life.More than a century later, India's self-styled Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has adopted a similarly unsettling symbol, not to tell a work of fiction, but to express the frustrations of a generation increasingly unsure whether years of education, expensive coaching and relentless competition will ever translate into a stable job.What began as a social media sensation with a strong and straightforward satirical structure, quickly evolved into one of the country's biggest youth-led movements in recent years.Calling itself the "voice of the lazy and unemployed," the movement grew from memes mocking joblessness, paper leaks, inflation and the political establishment into street protests.The protest may have become a trigger for a generation already grappling with shrinking employment opportunities, rising educational costs and growing uncertainty about the future.According to veteran economist Arun Kumar , a retired professor at JNU, "This unemployment crisis has created a huge gap between expectations and reality.""Young people earn degrees believing they will secure good jobs, but when those jobs do not materialise, they continue preparing for competitive examinations year after year. Many take these exams four, five or even six times because they still hope to secure an organised sector job.Their parents also encourage them because they know such jobs offer stable salaries and social security," he said."But the increasing privatisation of education has intensified competition. Coaching institutes want to showcase high success rates because that is their biggest selling point. That creates incentives for unethical practices, including paper leaks. The greater the privatisation, the greater the pressure to resort to illegal methods to ensure students succeed. Fake degrees, cheating and question paper leaks are all symptoms of a much deeper problem. They are linked to unemployment and the shortage of quality jobs in the organised sector," he added.India has spent decades expanding access to higher education. Universities have multiplied, enrollment has surged and millions of families have invested heavily in degrees, viewing education as the surest path to upward mobility.The numbers tell a remarkable story. According to the State of Working India 2026 report by Azim Premji University, the number of young graduates in India increased nearly 13-fold, rising from around 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023.But while the supply of graduates has grown rapidly, employment opportunities have not kept pace.The report estimates that graduate unemployment among people below the age of 25 is now close to 40%, while graduates accounted for nearly two-thirds of India's unemployed population in 2023.Even more striking is the rise in the number of unemployed graduates, which has increased from less than one million in 1983 to around 11 million in 2023, a 16-fold increase over four decades.The mismatch between education and employment has widened steadily since the mid-2000s as higher education expanded much faster than the creation of quality jobs. For millions of families, earning a college degree no longer guarantees stable employment or financial security.Recent government data suggest that the challenge is becoming even more severe.According to the government's flagship Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 rose to 16.2% in June, the highest level recorded since monthly estimates became available in April 2025. At that time, youth unemployment stood at 13.8%.The ministry of statistics and programme implementation (MoSPI) has cautioned that monthly figures may fluctuate because of seasonal factors, academic cycles and the increased frequency of surveys.Even so, the latest numbers are significant because they fit into a broader pattern rather than representing an isolated spike. Youth unemployment has increased across all six categories tracked by the survey, urban and rural areas, men and women alike, during the 15 months for which monthly data are available.At the same time, the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) among young people has declined from 42.7% to 40.3%. In simple terms, fewer young people are actively looking for work.Ordinarily, such a decline would be expected to reduce unemployment because fewer people are participating in the labour market. Instead, unemployment has continued to rise, suggesting that the economy is not generating enough opportunities even for the shrinking pool of job seekers.Annual PLFS data reinforce the same trend. Between 2022 and 2025, youth unemployment increased in 13 states and Union Territories, including Andhra Pradesh, Delhi, Telangana and West Bengal.The situation appears even more challenging for young women, with unemployment rising across 16 states and Union Territories during the same period.Taken together, the figures suggest that youth unemployment is becoming a structural challenge rather than a temporary fluctuation.Headline unemployment figures often fail to capture the deeper challenges within India's labour market. Many graduates do find work, but not necessarily the kind of work they expected after spending years in higher education.Economist Arun Kumar said that the root of the problem is the sharp divide between India's organised and unorganised sectors."When unemployment rises, it inevitably leads to greater conflict because there are too few jobs for too many people. In India, this problem is even more pronounced because the unorganised sector employs around 94% of the workforce, while the organised sector employs only about 6%. The difference in wages and job security between these two sectors is enormous. A courier delivery worker may earn around Rs 10,000-12,000 a month, whereas a postman can earn around Rs 70,000. Naturally, nobody wants to lose an organised sector job, and everyone wants to secure one. That intense competition creates immense pressure," he added.An analysis of India's Periodic Labour Force Survey illustrates this disconnect. Out of every 100 graduates aged between 15 and 29, only 50 are employed, 15 remain unemployed while actively searching for work, and the remaining 35 are outside the labour force altogether.Some continue their education. Others perform unpaid domestic work or have simply stopped looking for employment after repeated disappointments.Even among those who are employed, the quality of jobs remains a major concern. Only 26 out of every 100 graduates have regular salaried jobs. More strikingly, just four hold formal jobs that provide written contracts, paid leave and social security benefits.The remaining graduates are spread across self-employment, unpaid family work, casual labour and small household enterprises. Many earn irregular incomes and lack job security despite years spent pursuing higher education.The figures highlight a growing reality in India's labour market: employment alone is no longer an adequate measure of economic well-being. The challenge is increasingly about the availability of secure, productive and reasonably paid jobs.The employment crisis begins long before students enter the labour market. Competition for limited seats in prestigious colleges has transformed education itself into an expensive investment.Government survey data show that Indian households now spend a significantly larger share of their education budgets on private coaching than they did seven years ago.The sharpest increase has been among higher secondary students preparing for engineering, medical and university entrance examinations.Families now spend nearly one-fourth of their higher secondary education budgets on coaching, compared with about 18% in 2018.Private coaching expenses have also increased steadily across primary, middle and secondary education, reflecting a growing belief that classroom teaching alone is no longer sufficient to compete in high-stakes entrance examinations.The pressure becomes particularly visible in engineering education. India had around 4.4 million undergraduate engineering students during the 2023-24 academic year. Yet the country's top 100 engineering institutions together offered only about 500,000 seats.In effect, only one in nine engineering students can study at an institution widely regarded as offering strong placements and better career prospects.Students who fail to secure admission to elite institutions often graduate from colleges with weaker placement records, making it significantly harder to obtain well-paying jobs.The widening gap between educational aspirations and employment outcomes has created growing frustration among young people. The traditional promise that more education automatically leads to better employment is becoming increasingly uncertain.According to the State of Working India 2026 report, fewer than 7% of male graduates secure a permanent salaried job within one year of graduating. The figure is even lower, just 3.7%, when it comes to white-collar jobs.Using data from the PLFS and the earlier Employment-Unemployment Survey, the report estimates that 1.1 crore out of India's 6.3 crore graduates aged between 20 and 29 were unemployed in 2023.Graduate unemployment itself is not a new phenomenon. The report estimates that unemployment among graduates below the age of 25 increased from 35.02% in 1983 to 39.33% in 2023.What has changed, however, is the scale of the problem. India now produces far more graduates than ever before, while simultaneously entering the most important phase of its demographic transition.The country's median age currently stands at around 29 years and is expected to rise to 38 years by 2050.This is the period during which India's working-age population is expected to drive economic growth. If the economy fails to generate enough productive employment during this demographic window, the much-discussed demographic dividend could gradually turn into a demographic challenge.India today is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. Even amid geopolitical tensions, volatile oil prices and slowing global trade, the country has continued to post robust GDP growth and position itself as a manufacturing and investment hub.The government has invested heavily in highways, airports, railways, ports and digital infrastructure. Global technology companies such as Apple have expanded manufacturing in India, electronics exports have surged and semiconductor investments are beginning to gather pace.Policymakers increasingly see manufacturing as the sector that can absorb millions of workers and turn India's demographic advantage into sustained economic growth.Yet for many young Indians entering the labour market, this optimism feels distant. The central contradiction facing the Indian economy is that rapid economic growth has not translated into an equivalent expansion in quality employment.Economists often describe this phenomenon as "jobless growth", an economy that continues to grow without creating enough secure and productive jobs.India's challenge is especially daunting because nearly eight million graduates enter the labour market every year. Generating employment for such a large number of educated young people has become one of the country's biggest economic challenges.This gap between economic growth and employment opportunities lies at the heart of the frustration that has fuelled recent youth protests.Whether India is creating enough jobs depends largely on which dataset is examined. The Reserve Bank of India's KLEMS database estimated that the economy generated 4.7 crore jobs during 2023-24, the highest annual increase in more than four decades.However, labour economists caution against looking at headline employment numbers alone.Employment estimates differ across official surveys because they use different methodologies. More importantly, the definition of employment itself often masks the underlying quality of jobs being created.For instance, India's labour surveys classify a person as employed if they have worked even for a few days during the reference period.Likewise, unpaid family workers and subsistence self-employed individuals are counted as employed despite earning little or no regular income.As a result, headline employment figures may paint a healthier picture than what many young workers experience in reality. Increasingly, economists argue that the more important question is no longer how many jobs India is creating, but what kind of jobs they are.For decades, India's informal economy acted as a safety valve for the labour market. Workers unable to secure formal employment often found opportunities in small businesses, family enterprises, retail trade or self-employment.However, even this safety net appears to be weakening.According to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation's latest Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), the informal sector generated around 74.5 lakh jobs in 2025, significantly lower than the 1.1 crore jobs created during the previous survey period ending September 2024.Wage growth has also slowed sharply. Average wage growth in the sector declined to 3.9%, compared with 13% previously, suggesting that even workers who manage to find employment are seeing slower improvements in earnings.The figures reinforce concerns that employment opportunities are weakening across both formal and informal sectors, making it increasingly difficult for young people to find stable livelihoods.India's labour market also differs from many comparable economies because of the quality of employment available.International comparisons reveal another structural weakness: the quality of employment. Labour market studies show that around 93% of employed workers in Russia hold regular jobs. The share is about 68% in Brazil, 54% in China and 42% in Bangladesh, the PLFS 2022-23 & Jan-Mar 2024 data reported.In India, by contrast, only about 23% of workers are in regular salaried employment.This means that nearly three-fourths of Indian workers remain outside the formal sector, without written contracts, paid leave, provident fund benefits or social security.The shortage of secure employment also explains the extraordinary demand for government jobs. Whether it is railways, banking, the armed forces, civil services or state recruitmentexaminations, millions of candidates compete for relatively few vacancies because government employment still offers something much of the private sector cannot consistently provide stability.A government job often brings predictable salaries, pensions, housing allowances, healthcare benefits and long-term security.For many young Indians, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, these jobs represent far more than employment. They represent financial stability for entire families.According to Kumar, the desperation is visible in the jobs educated Indians are willing to apply for.Even as India grapples with creating quality jobs, technological change is reshaping the employment landscape.A government-backed research group estimates that artificial intelligence could displace around three million managerial and coding jobs by the end of this decade.Automation is expected to reduce demand for routine white-collar work at a time when India is producing record numbers of engineering and technology graduates.Overseas opportunities are also becoming more limited. Tighter immigration policies in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia have reduced opportunities for skilled Indian professionals.For decades, migration acted as a safety valve for India's educated workforce. That pathway is becoming increasingly uncertain."Many young Indians even leave the country in search of better opportunities. Some spend lakhs of rupees to migrate, while others take illegal routes because they see very few prospects at home. In many cases, they still end up doing low-paying or menial jobs abroad. That reflects the level of desperation created by the lack of opportunities in India,"Kumar noted on the brain-drain situation in India.India possesses one of the world's youngest populations, a demographic advantage that economists have long viewed as one of the country's greatest strengths.A growing working-age population has the potential to accelerate economic growth, boost productivity and expand domestic consumption.But demographic dividends are never automatic. They depend on whether an economy can generate enough productive employment for the millions entering the labour market every year.Research suggests that India's employment intensity of growth, the ability of economic expansion to generate jobs has steadily declined over the past four decades.Against this backdrop, the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak became much more than an examination controversy. Millions of students spend months and often years preparing for the country's most competitive entrance examinations.Families invest heavily in coaching classes, relocate to education hubs and, in many cases, students take gap years in pursuit of a medical seat.When allegations emerged that the examination paper had been leaked and sold before the test, the issue struck at the heart of a system that already demanded enormous financial and emotional investment.The government cancelled the examination, handed the investigation to the Central Bureau of Investigation and ordered a re-examination.For lakhs of aspirants, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, the cancellation meant far more than repeating a test. It meant another year of uncertainty after months of preparation and considerable financial sacrifice.Some students performed worse in the re-examination. Others worried they had lost their best chance of securing admission. Reports of severe psychological stress and alleged student suicides linked to the controversy further intensified public anger.What began as protests against examination irregularities gradually evolved into a wider movement about education, unemployment and shrinking opportunities.It was in this atmosphere that the Cockroach Janta Party found resonance among young Indians. Initially known for satirical social media posts, the movement soon expanded into organised protests questioning paper leaks, unemployment, inflation and what participants described as the growing disconnect between educational aspirations and employment opportunities.The group's unusual symbol, the cockroach, captured widespread attention.The insect represented resilience, survival and invisibility, mirroring how many young people felt overlooked despite years of education and preparation. Eventually, the protests became one of the biggest youth movements witnessed in recent years.The protests exposed far more than frustration over one examination. They revealed a widening disconnect between education, employment and economic expectations.Economist Arun Kumar says unemployment extends far beyond those who are officially counted as jobless."Youth unemployment, particularly among those aged 15 to 29, is extremely high, and the situation is especially difficult for women. There are different forms of unemployment. First, there are those actively looking for work but unable to find it. Second, there are people who are technically employed but only in low-paid, part-time or menial jobs that do not provide a decent livelihood," he said."Third, there is disguised unemployment, where people appear to be working but contribute little to productive economic activity. Finally, there are those who have stopped looking for work altogether because they have lost hope. Women are disproportionately represented in this last category. Female labour force participation in India remains much lower than in many other major economies, which means many women are no longer even counted among active job seekers," he added.Over the past few decades, India has dramatically expanded access to higher education, produced record numbers of graduates and remained one of the world's fastest-growing major economies.But the growth in quality jobs has failed to keep pace with the growing pool of educated youth. For many young Indians, securing a degree no longer guarantees a stable career or upward social mobility.That gap between aspirations and opportunities lies at the heart of the growing frustration. For millions of students, the question is no longer just whether examinations are conducted fairly.It is whether years of education, expensive coaching, repeated attempts at competitive exams and immense financial sacrifices will eventually lead to a secure, well-paying job. Without that, the frustrations exposed by such protests are likely to persist long after the headlines fade.
Article Summary: India produces millions of graduates every year but fails to create enough quality jobs. The problem isn't just unemployment, it's job quality. The increasing privatisation of education has intensified competition. Fake degrees, cheating and question paper leaks are all symptoms of a much deeper problem.

Article Title: The towel on the chair: How it became India's ultimate status symbol
Article Text:
In India, a towel draped over an office chair often became a symbol of power, associated with a govt job.

Corruption = Monopoly + discretion - accountability

Abhishek Asthana is a tech & media entrepreneur. He runs a creative agency called GingerMonkey & is also the Co-founder of

Knot Dating

, a VC funded matrimony startup.

Long ago, my father told me a story about a certain ‘ Sunil ji. Nobody ever addressed him by his first name, it was always succeeded by a ‘ji’, because his office chair was covered with a towel.He would often wear a safari suit & a stiff-upper lip at family weddings. The guy with a govt job, an Afsar (officer), top billing in the arranged marriage market, despite having the lowest basic pay. At one such wedding, his wife blurted out an issue they were facing. Due to some clerical mistake, the details of their salary account was not updated, and Sunil ji wasn’t receiving his salary for over 2 years. They found this anomaly just last month. My family was grudgingly impressed, and hoped one of their kids turned out to be a towel-chair guy like Sunil ji.For much of modern India’s history, there wasn't enough. Jobs. College seats. Telephones. Gas cylinders. Batsmen with a good strike rate. We were short of everything. As if our nation came out of British rule like some of the TV reporters came out of the NEET protest, Gasping for breath, barely surviving the violence with almost all of the valuables stolen, but their morality, virtue and the associated pride intact.This was India in 1947.Such was the muscle memory of the rule, that we kept presenting our Annual budget at 5 PM IST, so that our British overlords could tune-in after having their breakfast. This tradition continued till 1999, more than 50 years after independence, until the Finance minister Yashwant Sinha , changed it to 11 AM. Imagine. The trauma of British rule never went away, it showed up in our metabolic wiring, in our insulin resistance, in our early onset of diabetes. Primarily due to the British administered famines. The bodies of our ancestors rewired to store fat. When the Brits eventually went back, they left behind quite a few problematic things like bureaucracy, Pakistan & monumental scarcity.When our leaders took over, they knew our demand vastly exceeded the supply, so they had to control the access of resources. And who do you trust to do that?Another British inheritance - The Collectorate. A regiment of people specifically trained to extract from the population, to collect revenues and give it back to the overlords, for whom serving people was optional, a hobby. A lot of them were corrupt too, In contrast there was barely any corruption among British officers, because they were paid almost 70 times the Indian officers. Hence, the Indians had to compensate with corruption. As we know, they continued compensating beyond independence as well. This coterie was assigned to allocate resources to Indians.No wonder, they acquired tremendous power. People began paying to jump the queue. When the government decided who could manufacture, import or expand a factory, permissions themselves became valuable commodities. British raj was eventually succeeded by Inspector Raj. And the underpaid inspectors lived in the same bungalows the British lived in.Economist Robert Klitgaard famously summarized it as:Whenever one person has monopoly over a decision, wide discretion, and little accountability, corruption happens.Accountability was like Vitamin-D for the country. We were always deficient. Add to that a lethargic judiciary. Some even justified corruption saying it's an essential lubricant for files to move without friction. A tool to facilitate ease of doing business. Many of the Indian billionaires today, exist due to their ancestors greasing their file-folders with this lubricant generously.Corruption is a chronic illness, it has been embedded in the DNA of a drought-coded, resource starved nation like ours. A government comes to power riding a wave of public anger. The previous regime is portrayed as irredeemably corrupt. Files are opened. Committees are formed. Raids happen. People are content. Finally, someone is cleaning the system.For a while, it genuinely feels different. Time passes, Power stops feeling temporary. The government begins winning elections. The public approval remains high. Loyalists become more confident. Criticism starts sounding less like feedback and more like conspiracy. Every institution gradually fills up with people who think alike.Corruption creeps up again. Like a virus - a parasite that needs a host - like a mosquito or a bat or a pigeon.Parasites don't advertise themselves. They attach themselves to something stronger. In India's case, this host is often identity - caste, religion, language. Every political movement needs an emotional engine. That engine mobilises voters, creates loyalty and builds political capital. Most of the time these issues are legitimate and deeply important. But once emotions become intense enough, they also become excellent camouflage. People stop asking uncomfortable questions because larger battles appear to be underway.If my religion is under threat, why discuss the waterlogged street near my house?If my caste is finally receiving justice, why focus on procurement irregularities?Not saying, Identity is not important. But we often forget to see what’s lurking behind it. The virus keeps growing, and one day it becomes bigger than the host, voters can see it, and it gets overthrown. Exit pollsters get shamed. The power of democracy is lauded. Until a new host emerges. The cycle continues. Elections just change the wrapper of the age-old system.Corruption will go away when we make it high-risk and low-reward. High salaries & high conviction rate. A Singaporean minister earns more than a top investment banker. And their corruption watchdog has a conviction rate of 99%. Our ED has at ~1%. This is the crux, until we fix it - another Sunil ji will discover they have a salary account a decade later.
Article Summary: Abhishek Asthana is a tech & media entrepreneur. He runs a creative agency called GingerMonkey. He is also the Co-founder of. Knot Dating, a VC funded matrimony startup. He says bureaucracy breeds corruption in India.

Article Text:

NEW DELHI: When it comes to BJP ’s election playbook, there is always a method to the madness. Punjab , which votes early next year, appears to be following the same script.Sample these headlines:All these headlines, when looked at in isolation, appear to be one-off political developments separated in time. But one look at them together in the context of a wider long-term objective, they appear not just connected but also planned with a purpose. This is a perfect example of the BJP election playbook in action.The BJP, which over the years played second fiddle to the Akalis in Punjab, contested the 2022 elections alone after snapping ties with the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD). However, it could win only 2 seats with a vote share of 6.6%. Even the 2024 Lok Sabha elections were a huge disappointment. The BJP polled 18.65% of votes but could not win any seat. However, the BJP appears determined not to let the past numbers dictate its future strategy. And that explains the aggression with which the party has gone for the kill in Punjab.Punjab, which over the years alternated between the Congress and the Akalis, broke the duopoly in 2022 when it overwhelmingly voted for Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP.And that perhaps gives BJP its biggest hope as it marshals its resources. Now, let’s analyze all these headlines as a part of one story to understand how the BJP is gearing up to add another state to its ever-expanding kitty.When Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Punjab on February 1 this year, the BJP’s election playbook was already in action. The visit was part of a well thought-out and planned outreach that could increase the party’s base and presence in the state. The occasion was the 649th Birth Anniversary of Sant Guru Ravidas Ji. The Ravidassia community form an important electoral bloc of Punjab’s Scheduled Caste population, especially in the Doaba region.A slew of announcements were made, including renaming of Adampur Airport after Guru Ravidas and the launch of the Shri Guru Ravidas Ji Maharaj Express between Jalandhar and Varanasi. It was the start of a planned outreach. That outreach has continued with the Punjab BJP launching the statewide implementation of the 'Samrasta Sankalp Abhiyan' from July 29, the auspicious occasion of Guru Purnima, to commemorate the 650th birth anniversary year of Guru Ravidas Maharaj. Punjab BJP chief Kewal Singh Dhillon said the nationwide campaign will continue till February 20 (Magha Purnima) under the guidance of the BJP national leadership and aims to spread Guru Ravidas's timeless message of equality, dignity, social harmony and social justice across Punjab.The BJP, enriched by its experience from victories in states like West Bengal and Odisha, perhaps knows the importance of organisational strength in winning states. So in Punjab, after breaking its alliance with the Akalis, the BJP has been on an overdrive to build a strong local leadership. After the 2022 elections, several prominent Congress leaders had joined the BJP.And now in the run up to the 2027 electoral battle, seven AAP members of Rajya Sabha from the state are already a part of the party. And this acquisition includes Raghav Chaddha, once the most trusted associate of AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal. Chadha has a good understanding of the electoral thinking of AAP that rules Punjab now and can help the BJP capitalise on its weaknesses. As the elections approach, we could see Raghav Chaddha play a greater role in crafting and implementing BJP’s Punjab campaign.When the BJP replaced one Congress export Sunil Jakhar with another Kewal Singh Dhillon as its state chief, the change was aimed to send across a message. Dhillon, who is a seasoned politician and a prominent industrialist, became the first Jat Sikh to head the BJP in the state. The purpose was clear: outreach among Sikh voters to help increase the acceptability of the party after its Akali alliance ended. The BJP would hope that Dhillon could help the party expand its rural footprint. Besides Dhillon's political base is in Barnala, which falls in the Sangrur-Malwa region. This region is considered a stronghold of Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann and the Aam Aadmi Party.Ravneet Singh Bittu, who joined the BJP in March 2024 ahead of the general elections after ending his long association with the Congress, seems to have an important role in the saffron party’s blueprint for Punjab. During the 2024 campaign, Bittu was projected as an important Sikh face for the BJP by none other than Amit Shah. For those who remember, the entire BJP had rallied in support of Bittu after Rahul Gandhi had referred to him as “traitor”. The BJP made Bittu a minister in the Modi government and a member of Rajya Sabha despite his Lok Sabha election loss from Ludhiana in 2024 to showcase his importance. But after his RS tenure ended in June this year, he quit as minister amid hints that he will play a key role in BJP’s Punjab plans.According to reports, in June, Bittu had expressed his desire to work for Punjab in the Vidhan Sabha after spending nearly 17 years in Parliament. Bittu had then said that the BJP made him the minister even though he had lost the 2024 parliamentary elections."People of Punjab are fed up (with other parties). People are very much aware of development and progress taking place in other (BJP-ruled) states and they want prosperity in Punjab as well," Bittu had then said.Ravneet Singh Bittu is the grandson of former Punjab chief minister Beant Singh, who was assassinated in 1995. During his political career in the Congress, he was elected MP thrice and also served as the grand-old-party's leader in the Lok Sabha and as its whip in the Lower House.When Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Punjab for the second time on July 17, his focus was on development, youth and farmers. He pitched the BJP’s 'double-engine' model, arguing that a government of the same party at the Centre and in the state could bring investment, jobs and faster growth to Punjab.“Only the BJP can bring real change in Punjab. Only the BJP will make Punjab developed. Only the BJP will make Punjab self-reliant,” PM Modi said, adding that the state needed new investment, employment opportunities and greater global reach for products made in Punjab.He also accused the AAP government of stalling development and merely rebranding central schemes. Citing BJP-ruled Delhi and Haryana, Modi argued that Punjab too needed a 'double-engine' government, while claiming that farmers in the state were being denied the support available elsewhere.And while one part of PM Modi’s Punjab campaign was outreach, the other part was his fierce attack on the rivals in the state. Targeting the AAP government in Punjab over law and order and several other issues, PM Modi dubbed the ruling dispensation as a "Kattar Beiman" which neither has clean intentions, nor honesty.PM Modi then targeted the Congress, which has been in news more for factionalism than poll readiness. Taking a dig at infighting in the state unit over the chief minister's chair, the PM said "They are not fighting for people, they are fighting among themselves."Also under attack was the SAD, the BJP’s former ally. Taking a dig at the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD), the Prime Minister said it is not concerned about the welfare of the public as it is caught up with its own affairs.And finally, while the students’ protests against the NEET-UG paper leak forced Centre on the backfoot, the BJP is now using the same ammunition to target the Bhagwant Mann government over alleged paper leaks in Punjab.The BJP clearly has a plan for Punjab. It is bringing in leaders, strengthening its state organisation, reaching out to new social groups and sharpening its attack on both the AAP and the Congress. In the coming months, this push is likely to become more visible through political outreach, policy announcements and an aggressive campaign around governance, development and law and order.But activity alone does not guarantee electoral success. The BJP may have increased its vote share and political visibility, but it still has to expand beyond its traditional urban base, build trust in rural Punjab and convert imported leaders into an effective ground organisation.So, can it upset the AAP-Congress contest? It is still too early to say. The BJP will leave no stone unturned to make Punjab the 23rd state in its kitty. The real test will be whether its carefully assembled strategy can finally translate into seats.
Article Summary: The BJP contested the 2022 elections alone after snapping ties with the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) However, it could win only 2 seats with a vote share of 6.6%. Even the 2024 Lok Sabha elections were a huge disappointment. The BJP appears determined not to let the past numbers dictate its future strategy.

Article Title: Highway deaths dip in India for 1st time since Covid
Article Text: NEW DELHI: For the first time since the Covid pandemic, fatalities on national highways (NHs) declined last year, even as overall road deaths rose in India. Govt data submitted in Lok Sabha last week shows that deaths on NHs, including Centre-run expressways, fell by 4.1% to 62,122 in 2025 from 64,772 in 2024.Among states and UTs, 20 recorded a decline in fatalities on NHs while 15 reported an increase. Lakshadweep, with no national highways, was the only one to record ‘zero NH fatalities’ since 2022.Data shows UP registered the steepest decline in NH deaths, with fatalities dropping from 9,560 in 2024 to 7,573 in 2025. Madhya Pradesh also reported a significant reduction, from 4,644 to 3,610, along with Punjab, which logged a sharp fall from 1,562 to 1,022 during the same period.States that witnessed a rise in NH fatalities include Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and Gujarat.
Article Summary: For the first time since the Covid pandemic, fatalities on national highways (NHs) declined last year. Govt data submitted in Lok Sabha last week shows that deaths on NHs, including Centre-run expressways, fell by 4.1% to 62,122 in 2025 from 64,772 in 2024.

Assam continued to grapple with the aftermath of devastating floods on Sunday, with the death toll remaining at 82 and nearly 1.78 lakh people still affected across seven districts. Although floodwaters have begun to recede in some areas, thousands remain displaced, agricultural land is submerged, and the state government has intensified relief, rehabilitation and long-term mitigation efforts.According to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA), the flood situation has improved slightly, with the number of affected people declining from over 1.92 lakh to 1.78 lakh. However, 349 villages across Golaghat, Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Bajali, Dhemaji and Sonitpur districts remain affected.Charaideo is the worst-hit district, with more than 75,000 people affected, followed by over 58,000 in Sivasagar. Nearly 15,060 hectares of crop area remain submerged, while thousands of livestock have been affected or washed away.A total of 44 relief camps are currently sheltering around 15,000 displaced people, while another 17 relief distribution centres are providing assistance to more than 5,500 residents.The state government has directed district administrations to expedite the identification of affected families so that financial assistance can begin from August 3.One of the most remarkable rescue stories emerged from the Nepali Khuti area in Sivasagar district, where local villagers used six country-made boats to rescue more than 1,000 people from five villages after floodwaters rose rapidly on July 19.Residents said families were trapped on rooftops, elevated platforms and trees as water levels surged. The volunteer rescuers continued operations through the night despite having little food or water, ferrying stranded villagers to safer areas.Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma began a tour of the worst-hit districts on Sunday to oversee relief operations and prepare for a comprehensive damage assessment exercise scheduled to begin on August 9.The government has also directed officials to ensure uninterrupted distribution of relief kits, assess damage to educational institutions before schools reopen on August 10, and prepare restoration plans for damaged Namghars (Vaishnavite prayer centres).During his visit to erosion-hit areas of Dibrugarh district, including Chabua, Balijan, Pukhurijan, Dinjan and Rahmoria, Sarma announced that the state government will engage experts from IIT-Guwahati to develop a long-term solution to the Brahmaputra river’s erosion problem.Calling riverbank erosion one of Assam’s biggest geographical challenges, the chief minister said the state loses valuable land every year and that modern technology would be used to strengthen vulnerable riverbanks. The proposed IIT initiative will complement the government’s planned Rs 90 crore erosion mitigation project.Agriculture minister Pijush Hazarika visited Charaideo district on Sunday to review post-flood rehabilitation measures and launched community paddy nurseries and seedling distribution programmes for flood-affected farmers.The government said quality seedlings and other assistance would be provided to ensure cultivation resumes without delay during the current agricultural season.Support for flood-hit communities has continued to grow across Assam.Actor Randeep Hooda joined a relief drive organised by Global Sikhs in Sivasagar district, distributing essential supplies and serving food through langar for affected families. He warned that prolonged waterlogging and mud-filled homes could trigger disease outbreaks and urged people across the country to contribute to relief efforts.The Lok Janshakti Party (Ramvilas) has also launched a large-scale relief operation in Sivasagar, distributing food and essential supplies and announcing plans to feed up to 15,000 people daily for 10 days, along with setting up medical camps.The Centre has approved Rs 379.35 crore under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) for Assam’s flood response. Sarma thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah for extending assistance and for deploying Inter-Ministerial Central Teams to support relief and rehabilitation planning.Reliance Foundation has also contributed Rs 21 crore to the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund for flood relief and rehabilitation efforts.While water levels have started falling in parts of the state, the crisis is far from over. Thousands remain displaced, farmland continues to lie under water, and many families face the difficult task of rebuilding homes and livelihoods. Alongside immediate relief operations, the government is now focusing on compensation, agricultural recovery and long-term measures to address the recurring twin challenges of floods and Brahmaputra erosion.
Article Summary: The Centre has approved Rs 379.35 crore under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) for Assam’s flood response. Nearly 15,060 hectares of crop area remain submerged, while thousands of livestock have been affected or washed away. Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma began a tour of the worst-hit districts on Sunday.

Article Title: Students from around the world experience the Jain way of life in Rajasthan
Article Text:
Participants in the Jain Summer Program pose for a group photograph at Jain Vishwa Bharati in Ladnun, Rajasthan, on July 29. Photo by Aman Dhage/The American Bazaar

(By arrangement with

Nestled amid the arid plains of Rajasthan, about 230 miles west of Delhi, Ladnun is the kind of town many travelers might pass without a second glance. Its narrow streets, whitewashed temples, and unhurried pace stand in stark contrast to India’s bustling metropolitan centers.This summer, however, the quiet town has become an unlikely destination for seekers of one of the world’s oldest philosophies.For more than three centuries, Ladnun has been the spiritual home of the Terapanth order of Jainism, a reformist sect known for its disciplined monastic tradition and emphasis on nonviolence, self-restraint, and spiritual inquiry. Last month, those traditions welcomed an unusual group of visitors: nearly three dozen students, scholars, and faculty members from eight countries who are spending three weeks not merely studying Jainism, but living it.The immersive summer program, which began July 20 and concludes on Friday, is the result of a collaboration among Florida International University, California State University Long Beach, the Jain Education and Research Foundation (JERF), Jain Visva Bharati Institute, and southern California philanthropist Dr. Jasvant Modi, whose support made the initiative possible.Rather than treating Jainism as an academic subject confined to classrooms and textbooks, the organizers designed a program that allows participants to experience the philosophy through daily practice.Each morning began with meditation. Students attended lectures on Jain philosophy, Prakrit — the ancient language of many Jain scriptures — and the foundational principles of “Ahimsa” (nonviolence), “Anekantavada” (the multiplicity of viewpoints), and “Aparigraha” (non-attachment to possessions). They also interacted with monks and nuns, observed their disciplined routines, and experienced a lifestyle centered on simplicity, compassion, and mindfulness.“It has been a very eventful week, and it has been a tremendous experience,” said Anne Vallely, a professor at the University of Ottawa and one of the foremost scholars of Jainism in the Western world.Describing the demanding schedule, she added, “We have our lessons from 9:00 in the morning, and they go really into 10 o’clock, 11:00 at night.”The program reflects months of planning by scholars in India and the United States.Florida International University, home to the first endowed chairs in Jain Studies in the United States, worked closely with California State University Long Beach, to develop the curriculum. The Jain Education and Research Foundation helped coordinate the academic and logistical aspects of the initiative, while Jain Visva Bharati opened its sprawling campus and monastic community to the international participants.At the heart of the effort is a broader mission: introducing Jain philosophy to a global audience at a time when its central teachings of nonviolence, environmental sustainability, restraint, and respect for diverse perspectives have taken on renewed relevance.Much of that vision has been championed by physician, entrepreneur, and philanthropist Dr. Jasvant Modi, whose years of support for Jain education and higher learning have helped establish academic programs across the United States. Modi, who has contributed tens of millions of dollars to educational and religious causes in the United States, India, and globally, provided the principal financial support for this year’s summer school.“I was born in India in the Jain faith, and those principles of Ahimsa, compassion, and respect for all living beings have guided my entire life as a physician,” the La Cañada, California,-based physician entrepreneur told The American Bazaar. “⁠After my medical career, I realized philanthropy allows me to heal on a larger scale, not just one patient at a time. I contribute to Jain education because I believe America’s young students must be exposed to this ancient wisdom of tolerance, non-possessiveness, and plurality, which is so undervalued today. ”The program also coincided with another milestone.This year marks the 300th anniversary of the founding of the Terapanth order, giving participants an opportunity to witness commemorative events while learning about one of Jainism’s most influential traditions. Established in the 18th century by Acharya Bhikshu, the Terapanth order is distinguished by its centralized leadership and disciplined monastic structure. Its monks and nuns travel extensively to spread Jain teachings rather than remaining in permanent monasteries.Throughout the three weeks, students discovered that learning extended far beyond formal lectures.Meals became lessons in mindful eating. Silence became a form of reflection. Conversations with monks and nuns often continued long after scheduled sessions ended. Participants learned not only the philosophical foundations of Jainism but also how those principles shape everyday decisions, from food and consumption to conflict resolution and environmental responsibility.For many students, the immersive setting transformed abstract ideas into lived experience.“I’m surrounded by scholars and I’ve gotten to meet with sadhvis and sadhus, and it’s just been lovely,” said Carol Rodriguez, one of the participants, who holds a Ph.D. in Jain Studies from the University of Florida.The Cuban-born scholar earned her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Jain Studies from Florida International University in Miami, where she translated portions of the Lilavatisara, a 13th-century work by Jain monk Jinaratnasuri.The international composition of the group further enriched the discussions. Participants brought diverse academic backgrounds and cultural perspectives, creating conversations that reflected Jainism’s emphasis on dialogue and multiple viewpoints rather than absolute certainty.Organizers hope the program will serve as a model for future international collaborations in religious studies, philosophy, sustainability, and peace education.Unlike traditional study abroad programs, the Ladnun initiative invites participants to become temporary members of a living spiritual community, where learning occurs as much through observation and daily practice as through formal instruction.As the summer school concludes on July 7, participants will return to universities and communities around the world carrying more than lecture notes and academic credits. They will leave with firsthand experience of a philosophy that has quietly endured for millennia and memories of a small Rajasthan town where, for three weeks, Jainism was not simply studied, but lived.
Article Summary: Nearly three dozen students, scholars, and faculty members from eight countries are spending three weeks studying Jainism. The immersive summer program began July 20 and concludes on Friday. Participants interacted with monks and nuns, observed their disciplined routines, and experienced a lifestyle centered on simplicity, compassion, and mindfulness.

NEW DELHI: Around 158 cases related to alleged recruitment examination irregularities are pending trial in courts across the country despite the completion of investigations, with some cases dating back more than two decades, PTI reported.The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which probed these matters, has decided to approach high courts seeking the transfer of pending cases to fast-track courts being set up in several states to handle cases under the new anti-paper leak law.The agency will inform the high courts that it would provide dedicated special prosecutors and make all possible resources available to ensure the earliest possible conclusion of the trials.Government officials attributed the delays to the transfer of investigating officers, prosecutors, and even presiding judges.Delhi accounted for 25 alleged irregularity cases registered since 2000. These include the AIIMS PG recruitment examination case of 2010-11, the Delhi University Medical and Dental Entrance Examination case of 2011, CAT (Common Admission Test) irregularities of 2004, the SSC (Staff Selection Commission) recruitment case of 2013, and teachers' recruitment cases.Bihar has five pending cases, including three linked to the alleged NEET 2024 paper leak, besides irregularities in the PMT (Pre-Medical Test) examinations of 2003 and 2011.In Himachal Pradesh, the 2022 constable recruitment case is among three cases awaiting the start of trial. Jammu and Kashmir also has three pending cases, including alleged irregularities in junior engineer and constable recruitment.Similarly, five cases are awaiting trial in Jharkhand, five in Karnataka, three in Maharashtra — including two related to NEET 2024 — eight in Rajasthan, 14 in Tamil Nadu, and 10 each in West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh.The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026, recently passed by Parliament, provides for every state and Union territory to designate a sessions court as a special fast-track court in consultation with the chief justice of the concerned high court.The law mandates that these fast-track courts hear cases on a day-to-day basis without unnecessary adjournments, with trials to be completed within three months of the filing of the charge sheet. It also provides for the transfer of cases already pending before other courts to these newly designated special fast-track courts, where they are to be concluded within three months of transfer.Every state and Union territory will also appoint dedicated special public prosecutors to represent these cases.The legislation was enacted in the wake of the recent student protests at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, which culminated with the resignation of the-then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET (UG) paper leak in May. Protesters had also called for wider reforms in the country's examination system, following which the government constituted a high-powered task force, headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, to recommend reforms.
Article Summary: Around 158 cases related to alleged recruitment examination irregularities are pending trial in courts across the country. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is seeking the transfer of pending cases to fast-track courts being set up in several states. The legislation was enacted in the wake of the recent student protests.

Article Title: 'Dismantle terror infrastructure first': India's US envoy hits out at Pakistan over Indus Waters Treaty

India’s envoy to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra said Pakistan had eroded the foundation of the Indus Waters Treaty over the past five decades. He added that Islamabad had “dismantled” the goodwill and friendship that underpinned the 1960 agreement, and that New Delhi’s decision to keep the treaty in abeyance merely acknowledged that reality.As reported by US' Newsweek magazine, Kwatra said the treaty’s preamble reflected a commitment made 'in a spirit of goodwill and friendship', but Pakistan’s conduct had weakened that foundation over half a century.“It is worth remembering that the treaty's preamble declares it was concluded ‘in a spirit of goodwill and friendship’. Pakistan spent half a century dismantling that goodwill and friendship. The abeyance merely acknowledges what Pakistan's conduct had already destroyed,” Kwatra said.His remarks came after Pakistan recently hosted a conference protesting India’s decision to keep the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance on April 23 last year, a day after Pakistan-trained terrorists killed 26 people in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir.The IWT, signed by India and Pakistan in 1960, divided the waters of the six rivers of the Indus basin between the two countries. India was given control over the eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej which account for about 20 per cent of the basin’s water, while Pakistan received rights over the western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab carrying around 80 per cent.“That asymmetry stifled development for decades in Indian regions that could have benefited from better water rights. India honoured the treaty anyway,” Kwatra said according to Newsweek.The envoy said Pakistan’s approach towards India had been marked by wars, hostility and cross-border terrorism, citing the 1965, 1971 and 1999 conflicts along with major terror attacks, including the 2001 Parliament attack, the 2008 Mumbai attacks, the 2016 Uri and Pathankot attacks, the 2019 Pulwama attack and the 2025 Pahalgam attack.Kwatra also said that if Pakistan sincerely wanted India’s cooperation on bilateral issues, it must first dismantle the terror infrastructure it has built over the years.On implementation of the treaty, Kwatra alleged that Pakistan had repeatedly delayed Indian projects and opposed efforts to revisit the agreement in view of changing technology and requirements.“Pakistan also consistently blocked India's initiatives to renegotiate the treaty in light of six decades of technological change, which would have let India develop its hydropower potential,” Kwatra added.“Bit by bit, Pakistan eroded India's faith that it could exercise its rights under the treaty, or hope for a better one suited to today's realities,” he said.Responding to calls for India and Pakistan to resume talks, Kwatra said past initiatives had failed to address core concerns.“Prime Minister Narendra Modi has clearly voiced India’s stand today: ‘Terror and talks cannot go together... Terror and trade cannot go together... Water and blood cannot flow together',” Kwatra said.Kwatra also said Pakistan should focus on improving its own water management instead of blaming India for its challenges."The Government of Pakistan would do better to fix its dismal water productivity, than to stage conferences blaming India and issuing threats,” he said, adding, “The habit of pinning every domestic failure on India has grown old."
